about.title: Irvine Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Irvine's workforce is spread across research campuses, medical offices, distribution centers and active construction sites. When someone is hurt doing that work, California generally routes the claim through workers' compensation, which pays regardless of fault but also limits what you can recover from your employer. What many people in Orange County don't hear is that a second path may exist. If a subcontractor, a property owner, defective equipment or another driver caused the harm, a separate injury claim against that third party can run alongside the comp case. Irvine recorded 910 injury collisions in 2025, with 1,233 people hurt and 10 lives lost, and public records show crashes clustering along I-5, I-405 and Culver Drive, often on Friday evenings between 5 and 7 p.m. A delivery driver or field technician struck during a shift may have both a comp claim and a claim against the at-fault motorist. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm; an independent attorney can help sort out which path fits your situation.

items.title: Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker or driver can be held responsible separately. An attorney in our network can look for that second claim.

items.title: Deadlines You Shouldn't Miss
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and a third-party injury claim generally carries a two-year deadline. Getting connected early keeps both clocks in view.

items.title: Protection Against Pushback
items.desc: It is illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you're worried about your job, that concern is worth raising with an attorney right away.

items.question: I was rear-ended on I-405 while making deliveries for my Irvine employer. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It may be both. Because you were working, your medical bills and lost wages typically flow through workers' compensation no matter who caused the crash. Because another driver was negligent, you may also have a separate injury claim against that motorist, which can cover losses comp does not. An attorney can evaluate how the two fit together.

items.question: Can I sue my employer if the injury was clearly their fault?
items.answer: In most cases, no. California makes workers' compensation the exclusive remedy against your employer, and fault is not part of that system. The exceptions are narrow, so the more common route to additional recovery is a claim against a negligent third party.

items.question: What if I waited a few weeks before telling anyone at work about my injury?
items.answer: Report it as soon as you can. California expects notice to your employer within 30 days, and a late report can complicate a comp claim even if it doesn't always end it. Any third-party claim runs on its own two-year deadline, so a delay in reporting doesn't automatically close that door.
